questions.stem: In this diagram of the vagus and phrenic nerves in the thorax, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is shown hooking around a specific structure before ascending back to the larynx. This anatomical relationship explains why left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness) can result from which of the following?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A thyroid nodule at the level of the cricoid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compression of the phrenic nerve at the diaphragm

choices.label: E
choices.text: An aortic arch aneurysm or mass at the aortopulmonary window

explanation.summary: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta at the ligamentum arteriosum, so pathology at the aortic arch or aortopulmonary window can stretch or compress it, producing hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).
explanation.whyCorrect: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the arch of the aorta at the ligamentum arteriosum, so pathology at the aortic arch or aortopulmonary window can stretch or compress it, producing hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A right apical Pancoast tumor can involve the right recurrent laryngeal nerve, which loops around the right subclavian artery, not the left nerve.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An abdominal aortic aneurysm lies below the diaphragm, far from the recurrent laryngeal nerves, which loop in the root of the neck and upper thorax.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A thyroid nodule can injure either recurrent laryngeal nerve in the neck, but that relationship has nothing to do with the nerve hooking around a thoracic structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phrenic nerve controls the diaphragm, and compressing it causes diaphragmatic paralysis, not hoarseness; it does not carry laryngeal fibers.

questions.stem: This posterior mediastinal dissection shows a muscular tube descending behind the heart, crossed by a nerve plexus and passing through the diaphragm. Which structure is the central tubular organ shown running from the neck to the abdomen?

explanation.whyCorrect: The figure traces the esophagus from its cervical part through the thorax (surrounded by the esophageal plexus formed by the vagus nerves) to its abdominal part after passing through the diaphragmatic hiatus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The azygos vein ascends along the right side of the vertebral bodies and arches over the right lung root into the SVC; it is not a muscular tube surrounded by a vagal plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The descending thoracic aorta runs left of the vertebral column and passes behind the diaphragm through the aortic hiatus at T12, not through the muscular esophageal hiatus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The thoracic duct is a thin lymphatic channel that runs between the aorta and azygos vein; it is not a thick muscular tube wrapped by the esophageal plexus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The trachea is a cartilage-ringed airway that ends at the carina around T4-T5; it does not descend behind the heart or pass through the diaphragm.

questions.stem: This cadaveric dissection of an opened thorax with the lungs removed exposes the central compartment between the two pleural cavities. What region of the body is displayed?

whyWrongByChoice.B: The posterior abdominal wall lies below the diaphragm; this dissection shows the thoracic compartment between the pleural cavities.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The axilla is the pyramidal space between the arm and lateral chest wall; it is not the central thoracic compartment between the lungs.

questions.stem: This illustration highlights a nerve looping beneath a fibrous remnant near the aortic arch. What embryologic vessel does the ligamentum arteriosum represent, and what is its clinical relevance to the adjacent nerve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the remnant of the ductus arteriosus, and the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the remnant of the foramen ovale draining into the atrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a persistent left superior vena cava that compresses the phrenic nerve

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the obliterated ductus venosus supplying the esophagus

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the remnant of the umbilical vein and unrelated to any nerve

explanation.summary: The ligamentum arteriosum is the postnatal remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the arch just lateral to it, so an aortic aneurysm or mass here can entrap the nerve and cause hoarseness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The ligamentum arteriosum is the postnatal remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the arch just lateral to it, so an aortic aneurysm or mass here can entrap the nerve and cause hoarseness.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The foramen ovale is an interatrial opening whose remnant is the fossa ovalis inside the heart, not a fibrous cord at the aortic arch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A persistent left superior vena cava is a venous anomaly that usually drains into the coronary sinus; it is not a fibrous ligament and does not compress the phrenic nerve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ductus venosus shunted blood through the liver and becomes the ligamentum venosum; it has no connection to the aortic arch or esophagus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The umbilical vein becomes the ligamentum teres hepatis in the falciform ligament of the abdomen, not a structure at the aortic arch.

questions.stem: In this anterior view of the opened thorax, a lobulated glandular structure sits in the superior/anterior mediastinum just deep to the manubrium, overlying the great vessels and pericardium. In an adult this organ is typically atrophied, but what is it?

explanation.summary: The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium; prominent in children, it involutes with age. Its location makes it a common source of anterior mediastinal masses (e.g., thymoma).
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus lies in the anterior mediastinum behind the manubrium; prominent in children, it involutes with age. Its location makes it a common source of anterior mediastinal masses (e.g., thymoma).

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pericardial fat pad sits at the cardiophrenic angles near the diaphragm, not as a lobulated gland behind the manubrium over the great vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The thyroid gland lies in the neck anterior to the trachea at C5-T1; only a retrosternal goiter extends down, and it is not the normal resident of this space.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The parathyroid glands are tiny, rice-grain-sized bodies on the posterior thyroid, far too small to form a lobulated mass over the great vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A lymph node mass would be an abnormal finding; the normal lobulated organ of the anterior mediastinum that involutes with age is the thymus.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Directly into the superior vena cava

choices.label: E

whyWrongByChoice.C: The thoracic duct runs beside the azygos vein in the posterior mediastinum but does not empty into it; it continues up to the left side of the neck.

whyWrongByChoice.E: The right jugulosubclavian junction receives the right lymphatic duct, which drains only the right upper quadrant of the body, not the thoracic duct.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lymphatic drainage of the mediastinum

choices.label: C
choices.text: The distribution of the vagus nerve branches

choices.label: E

explanation.whyCorrect: The figure illustrates the mediastinal lymph node stations; knowledge of these groups underlies cancer staging, as tumor spread to specific nodal stations determines resectability and prognosis.

questions.stem: This lateral schematic divides the mediastinum into compartments using a horizontal plane. The dashed line separating the superior mediastinum from the inferior compartments passes through which surface landmark?

explanation.summary: The transverse thoracic plane runs from the sternal angle (angle of Louis) posteriorly to the T4/T5 disc, dividing the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts; the inferior is further split into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments.
explanation.whyCorrect: The transverse thoracic plane runs from the sternal angle (angle of Louis) posteriorly to the T4/T5 disc, dividing the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts; the inferior is further split into anterior, middle, and posterior compartments.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The jugular notch sits at about T2 on the superior border of the manubrium, above the plane that separates the superior and inferior mediastinum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The costal margin at rib 10 lies at the lower boundary of the thorax, far below the mediastinal dividing plane.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The clavicular midpoint is the landmark for the midclavicular line, a vertical reference, not the horizontal plane dividing the mediastinum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The xiphisternal joint marks the lower end of the sternal body at about T9, near the inferior border of the mediastinum.

questions.imageRef: repic-068_Brick Exchange - Mediastinum (Part 1 of 2)_p4_2.png

questions.stem: In this lateral cadaveric view of the inferior mediastinum, the dashed outline lies between the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind. Which mediastinal compartment contains mainly the heart and roots of the great vessels?

explanation.summary: The inferior mediastinum is subdivided into anterior (sternum to pericardium), middle (the pericardium and its contents, i.e., heart and great vessel roots), and posterior (behind the pericardium, containing esophagus and descending aorta).
explanation.whyCorrect: The inferior mediastinum is subdivided into anterior (sternum to pericardium), middle (the pericardium and its contents, i.e., heart and great vessel roots), and posterior (behind the pericardium, containing esophagus and descending aorta).

whyWrongByChoice.B: The superior mediastinum lies above the sternal angle plane and contains the aortic arch, trachea and thymus, not the heart itself.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The anterior mediastinum is the narrow space between the sternum and pericardium; it holds thymic remnants, fat and nodes, not the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The retropharyngeal space lies behind the pharynx in the neck and continues only into the superior mediastinum; it does not contain the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the pericardium and holds the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos vein and thoracic duct.

explanation.whyCorrect: The plane of the sternal angle (transverse thoracic plane, T4/T5) marks the beginning and end of the aortic arch, the bifurcation of the trachea, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The xiphoid process at about T9 marks the lower sternum, well below the aortic arch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The diaphragm at T10 is where the esophagus passes through its hiatus; the aorta passes at T12, and neither marks the arch.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The carina sits at the sternal angle plane, about T4-T5, in most adults; T7 is too low for the level at which the aortic arch begins and ends.

questions.imageRef: repic-070_Brick Exchange - Mediastinum (Part 1 of 2)_p7_1.png

questions.stem: In a patient with a mediastinal mass obstructing the vessel labeled at the upper right of this venous diagram (the superior vena cava), which vein provides the most important collateral route returning blood to the heart?

explanation.summary: The azygos system connects the SVC and IVC territories along the posterior thoracic wall. In SVC obstruction it becomes the key collateral channel, allowing upper-body venous blood to bypass the block and reach the right atrium.
explanation.whyCorrect: The azygos system connects the SVC and IVC territories along the posterior thoracic wall. In SVC obstruction it becomes the key collateral channel, allowing upper-body venous blood to bypass the block and reach the right atrium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The portal vein carries splanchnic blood to the liver and forms portosystemic collaterals in portal hypertension; it is not the main bypass for SVC obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The coronary sinus drains the heart's own veins into the right atrium; it does not receive blood from the head, neck or arms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The internal thoracic artery is an artery, so it cannot provide venous return; its companion internal thoracic veins are only a secondary collateral pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium and do not connect to the systemic veins blocked by an SVC obstruction.

questions.imageRef: repic-071_Brick Exchange - Mediastinum (Part 1 of 2)_p8_1.png

questions.stem: This cadaveric dissection of the superior mediastinum shows the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. Around which structure does this nerve loop before ascending to the larynx?

explanation.whyCorrect: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch just lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum. Its long thoracic course explains hoarseness from aortic aneurysm, left atrial enlargement, or mediastinal tumor (Ortner syndrome).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pulmonary veins enter the left atrium in the lung hilum; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve does not loop around them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The superior vena cava is a right-sided structure; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around a left-sided arterial structure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The right subclavian artery is where the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops; the left nerve descends lower, into the thorax.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brachiocephalic artery lies to the right of the trachea; neither recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath it.

questions.imageRef: repic-072_Brick Exchange - Mediastinum (Part 1 of 2)_p9_1.png

questions.stem: These frontal and lateral chest radiographs plus a sagittal CT all point to an opacity located just behind the sternum. In which mediastinal compartment is this lesion located?

explanation.summary: A retrosternal mass filling the space in front of the pericardium and great vessels localizes to the anterior mediastinum, the classic site for the 'terrible Ts' (thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma).
explanation.whyCorrect: A retrosternal mass filling the space in front of the pericardium and great vessels localizes to the anterior mediastinum, the classic site for the 'terrible Ts' (thymoma, teratoma, thyroid, lymphoma).

whyWrongByChoice.C: The posterior mediastinum lies behind the heart beside the spine, where neurogenic tumors occur, not immediately behind the sternum.

questions.stem: This patient shows facial fullness/plethora and prominent dilated superficial veins over the upper chest wall. This appearance is the classic presentation of which condition?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Right heart failure with peripheral edema

explanation.summary: Obstruction of the SVC (commonly by a mediastinal tumor such as lung cancer or lymphoma) impairs venous return from the head, neck, and upper chest, producing facial plethora/edema and engorged collateral chest wall veins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Obstruction of the SVC (commonly by a mediastinal tumor such as lung cancer or lymphoma) impairs venous return from the head, neck, and upper chest, producing facial plethora/edema and engorged collateral chest wall veins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cushing syndrome causes a round moon face with a dorsocervical fat pad and purple striae, from fat redistribution rather than engorged chest wall collateral veins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Right heart failure raises systemic venous pressure, causing jugular venous distension and dependent leg edema, rather than facial plethora with dilated chest wall collaterals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anaphylactic angioedema causes sudden swelling of the lips, tongue and eyelids with urticaria, with no dilated superficial chest veins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Caput medusae is periumbilical venous distension from portal hypertension, found on the abdomen and not with facial plethora.

questions.stem: This coronal CT shows a lung cancer with soft tissue encircling a large thin-walled venous structure to the right of the ascending aorta. Obstruction of the encased vessel would most directly cause which clinical syndrome?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aortic dissection with limb pulse deficits

explanation.whyCorrect: The tumor wraps around the superior vena cava; malignant compression or invasion of the SVC obstructs venous return from the head, neck, and arms, producing SVC syndrome. Lung cancer is the most common cause.

whyWrongByChoice.D: Aortic dissection is an intimal tear in the aortic wall; the encased vessel is a thin-walled vein beside the aorta, not the aorta itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiac tamponade results from pericardial fluid compressing the heart, not from tumor encasing a mediastinal vein.

questions.stem: This chest radiograph shows a large thoracic aortic aneurysm with prominent aortic arch. If this patient develops new hoarseness, stretching or compression of which nerve is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Left vagus nerve trunk in the neck

explanation.whyCorrect: Because the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch, an expanding arch aneurysm stretches it, paralyzing the left vocal cord and producing hoarseness (Ortner cardiovocal syndrome).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The left vagus trunk in the neck lies above the aortic arch, so an arch aneurysm stretches the recurrent branch that hooks under the arch, not the cervical trunk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the posterior tongue taste, carotid sinus and stylopharyngeus; its course in the neck is far from the aortic arch.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hypoglossal nerve is motor to the tongue; injury causes tongue deviation, not hoarseness, and it does not enter the thorax.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The right phrenic nerve supplies the right hemidiaphragm; compression causes diaphragmatic elevation, not vocal cord paralysis.

choices.label: E

questions.stem: This anterior view of the thoracic wall veins highlights the azygos and hemiazygos system. What is the principal functional role of this venous system?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: E

questions.imageRef: repic-076_Brick Exchange - Mediastinum (Part 2 of 2)_p3_1.png

questions.stem: This diagram of the thoracic aorta and its branches shows the ligamentum arteriosum near the arch. This fibrous cord is the postnatal remnant of which fetal structure?

questions.stem: This chest radiograph is paired with drained pleural fluid shown as milky-white bottles. What is this fluid, and what does it indicate?

choices.label: E

questions.stem: This illustration of esophageal lymphatic drainage shows nodes along the entire esophagus. Why does esophageal carcinoma frequently produce widely scattered (skip) nodal metastases?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Esophageal lymph drains exclusively to a single sentinel node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymph flows only downward toward the celiac nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The esophagus has no lymphatic drainage, so tumor spreads only hematogenously

choices.label: D
choices.text: The esophagus has an extensive, longitudinally interconnected submucosal lymphatic plexus

choices.label: E

questions.stem: Using the cardiac outline traced on these PA and lateral chest radiographs, above what cardiothoracic ratio is the heart considered enlarged?

questions.stem: This echocardiogram shows an anechoic (black) fluid rim surrounding all four chambers. If this collection accumulates rapidly, what life-threatening complication results?

explanation.summary: Fluid in the pericardial space (pericardial effusion) that accumulates faster than the sac can stretch raises intrapericardial pressure, compressing the chambers and impairing filling — cardiac tamponade, which causes obstructive shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluid in the pericardial space (pericardial effusion) that accumulates faster than the sac can stretch raises intrapericardial pressure, compressing the chambers and impairing filling — cardiac tamponade, which causes obstructive shock.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Infective endocarditis appears on echo as vegetations on valve leaflets, not as a fluid rim around the heart.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary embolism may dilate the right ventricle on echo, but it does not produce a pericardial fluid collection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Aortic dissection can bleed into the pericardium, but the fluid rim itself is an effusion, and its rapid build-up causes tamponade, not dissection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myocardial infarction shows regional wall-motion abnormalities, and a fluid rim is a complication rather than a cause of infarction.

questions.stem: This figure shows the fibrous trigones, interleaflet triangles, and membranous septum surrounding the four valve rings. What is the principal function of this cardiac fibrous skeleton?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Generates the pacemaker impulse of the heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: Actively contracts to eject blood from the ventricles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stores oxygen for the myocardium during systole

choices.label: E
choices.text: Provides the main blood supply to the myocardium

explanation.summary: The fibrous skeleton anchors the valves and forms a non-conducting barrier between atrial and ventricular myocardium, forcing impulses through the AV node/bundle of His and preventing direct atrioventricular electrical spread.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fibrous skeleton anchors the valves and forms a non-conducting barrier between atrial and ventricular myocardium, forcing impulses through the AV node/bundle of His and preventing direct atrioventricular electrical spread.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrous connective tissue cannot contract; ejection is done by ventricular myocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myocardial oxygen storage is handled by myoglobin in cardiomyocytes, not by the collagenous skeleton.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The myocardium is supplied by the coronary arteries arising from the aortic sinuses, not by the fibrous skeleton.

questions.stem: In this section the mitral valve is open, the aortic valve is closed, the chordae are loose, and the papillary muscle is relaxed. Which phase of the cardiac cycle is depicted?

explanation.summary: An open mitral (AV) valve with a closed aortic (semilunar) valve and relaxed papillary muscles allows the left ventricle to fill from the atrium — the defining configuration of ventricular diastole.
explanation.whyCorrect: An open mitral (AV) valve with a closed aortic (semilunar) valve and relaxed papillary muscles allows the left ventricle to fill from the atrium — the defining configuration of ventricular diastole.

whyWrongByChoice.A: In isovolumetric contraction both the mitral and aortic valves are closed while the papillary muscles tense, so the mitral valve would not be open.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Isovolumetric relaxation has both valves closed as ventricular pressure falls; the mitral valve has not yet opened.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Atrial repolarization is an electrical event hidden in the QRS complex, not a mechanical valve configuration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: In ejection the aortic valve is open and the mitral valve is closed with tense chordae, the opposite of what is shown.

questions.stem: In this coronal section of the heart, which chamber receives deoxygenated blood and pumps it into the pulmonary circulation?

explanation.whyCorrect: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is ejected through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries for oxygenation in the lungs.

questions.stem: This superior view of the valve plane (base of the heart) shows all four valves. Which valve prevents backflow of blood into the left atrium during ventricular systole?

explanation.summary: During ventricular systole the mitral (bicuspid) valve closes to prevent regurgitation of blood from the left ventricle back into the left atrium; the tricuspid does the same on the right side.

questions.stem: This dissection shows the papillary muscles connected to the AV valve leaflets by thin cords (chordae tendineae). What is the function of this papillary muscle–chordae apparatus?

choices.label: A

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anchors the great vessels to the pericardium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Opens the semilunar valves during ejection

choices.label: E

whyWrongByChoice.C: The LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove to supply the anterior wall and septum, not the right atrial SA node.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The left circumflex gives the SA nodal artery in only about 40% of people, a minority pattern.

questions.stem: This muscle tissue is composed of branching cells joined end to end, each with a single central nucleus and abundant pink cytoplasm, supported by delicate connective tissue and capillaries. What tissue is this?

explanation.whyCorrect: Branching fibers with single central nuclei and interposed capillaries are diagnostic of cardiac muscle, distinguishing it from multinucleated peripheral-nucleus skeletal muscle and spindle-shaped smooth muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dense regular connective tissue is parallel collagen bundles with flattened fibroblast nuclei, as in tendon, not branching contractile cells with pink cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Skeletal muscle fibers are long, unbranched and multinucleated with nuclei at the periphery, unlike these branching cells with single central nuclei.

questions.stem: The magnified inset (red arrow) highlights a darker transverse band crossing a cardiac muscle fiber at the junction between two cells. What structure is indicated, and what is its function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A motor end plate transmitting nerve impulses to the fiber

choices.label: B
choices.text: A band of collagen anchoring the cell to the endomysium

choices.label: C
choices.text: A T-tubule invagination triggering calcium release

choices.label: D
choices.text: An intercalated disc, which mechanically couples cardiomyocytes

choices.label: E

explanation.summary: Intercalated discs are specialized step-like junctions between cardiomyocytes containing desmosomes/fasciae adherentes (mechanical linkage) and gap junctions (electrical continuity), enabling the myocardium to contract as a functional syncytium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intercalated discs are specialized step-like junctions between cardiomyocytes containing desmosomes/fasciae adherentes (mechanical linkage) and gap junctions (electrical continuity), enabling the myocardium to contract as a functional syncytium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiac muscle has no motor end plates; its contraction is triggered by spread of action potentials from cell to cell, with autonomic nerves only modulating it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The endomysium is delicate connective tissue around each fiber; it does not form a dark step-like band crossing the fiber at a cell-cell junction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma, too fine to resolve by light microscopy, that run at the Z-lines within a cell, not at the boundary between two cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Z-lines are thin, regularly repeating lines within every sarcomere; the thicker, irregular band at the junction of two cells is an intercalated disc.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The endocardium lines the inner chamber surface with endothelium, not the outer surface with mesothelium, fat and nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The tunica media of a coronary artery is a ring of smooth muscle within a vessel wall, not a surface layer of the heart covered by mesothelium.

explanation.whyCorrect: The endocardium is the innermost layer lining the cardiac chambers and valves; its endothelium is continuous with that of vessels entering and leaving the heart.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The parietal pericardium lines the inner surface of the fibrous sac, outside the heart, not the chambers.

questions.stem: At the inner surface of this heart wall, the subendocardial layer (SEn) beneath the endocardium (En) contains clusters of large, pale-staining cells (P) with abundant clear cytoplasm sitting above the myocardium (M). What are these pale cells?

explanation.whyCorrect: Large, pale cells rich in glycogen within the subendocardial layer are Purkinje fibers, specialized conducting cardiomyocytes that rapidly distribute the electrical impulse to the ventricular myocardium.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The cardiac skeleton is dense fibrous connective tissue around the valve rings, not clusters of pale cells beneath the endocardium.

questions.stem: In this cross-section of the heart, blood returning from the systemic circulation via the vena cavae must pass through which valve to enter the right ventricle?

whyWrongByChoice.C: The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle and carries oxygenated pulmonary venous blood.

questions.stem: On this aortic pressure tracing, the brief downward deflection immediately following peak pressure marks which cardiac event?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Opening of the mitral valve during rapid filling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Opening of the aortic valve at the start of ejection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Closure of the mitral valve at the onset of systole

explanation.summary: The dicrotic notch is the small dip in the aortic pressure curve produced by a brief backflow and elastic recoil as the aortic valve snaps shut, marking the end of ventricular ejection and start of diastole.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dicrotic notch is the small dip in the aortic pressure curve produced by a brief backflow and elastic recoil as the aortic valve snaps shut, marking the end of ventricular ejection and start of diastole.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrial systole occurs at the end of diastole, before the aortic valve opens, and does not cause a notch in the aortic pressure tracing after peak ejection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitral opening comes later, at the end of isovolumetric relaxation, and appears on atrial and ventricular tracings rather than as a notch in aortic pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aortic valve opening marks the start of the aortic pressure upstroke, before the peak, not a dip after it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mitral closure happens at the start of isovolumetric contraction, while aortic pressure is still falling to its diastolic minimum, before ejection begins.

questions.stem: On this venous pressure tracing, the descent that occurs as the tricuspid valve is pulled down during ventricular systole (while the atrium relaxes) is labeled which wave?

explanation.whyCorrect: The x descent reflects the fall in atrial pressure during ventricular systole as the atrium relaxes and the tricuspid annulus is pulled downward; the y descent instead follows tricuspid opening and atrial emptying.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The a wave is a positive deflection from atrial contraction at the end of diastole, not a descent during ventricular systole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The y descent follows tricuspid opening, when blood empties from the atrium into the ventricle in early diastole.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The c wave is a small positive bump from tricuspid bulging into the atrium during isovolumetric contraction, not a fall in pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The v wave is the rise in atrial pressure from venous filling against a closed tricuspid valve late in systole, not a descent.

questions.stem: On this Wiggers diagram, the S1 heart sound coincides with which mechanical event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrial contraction producing the a wave

choices.label: B
choices.text: Opening of the mitral valve during rapid filling

choices.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves (S2)

choices.text: Opening of the aortic valve during rapid ejection

choices.text: Closure of the mitral (and tricuspid) valves

explanation.whyCorrect: S1 marks the beginning of systole and is produced by closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves as ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure; S2 corresponds to semilunar valve closure at the end of ejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrial contraction occurs just before S1 and may produce S4 in a stiff ventricle; it does not cause the first heart sound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitral opening at the start of rapid filling is normally silent; it is followed by S3 if the ventricle is volume-overloaded.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Semilunar valve closure produces S2 at the end of ejection, not S1.

questions.stem: On this combined pressure and LV volume tracing, ventricular volume reaches its minimum (ESV) immediately after which event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mitral valve closure at the start of isovolumetric contraction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Atrial contraction adding the final filling volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aortic valve closure at the end of ejection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitral valve opening at the start of filling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Aortic valve opening at the onset of ejection

explanation.summary: Ejection empties the ventricle until the aortic valve closes; at that point LV volume is at its lowest (end-systolic volume). Filling then resumes only after the mitral valve opens, raising volume back toward EDV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ejection empties the ventricle until the aortic valve closes; at that point LV volume is at its lowest (end-systolic volume). Filling then resumes only after the mitral valve opens, raising volume back toward EDV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At mitral valve closure the ventricle has just finished filling, so volume is at its maximum (end-diastolic volume), not its minimum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atrial contraction tops off ventricular filling, bringing volume up to end-diastolic volume, the opposite of the minimum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: When the mitral valve opens, volume is still at end-systolic volume; the minimum was reached earlier, when ejection stopped at aortic valve closure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: At aortic valve opening the ventricle still holds its full end-diastolic volume; ejection then reduces it.

questions.stem: In the normal S2 shown at the top, why does the A2-P2 split widen during inspiration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The mitral valve closes earlier during inspiration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased venous return delays pulmonic valve closure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Systemic vascular resistance falls during inspiration

explanation.summary: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, augmenting venous return to the right heart. The larger right ventricular volume prolongs right ventricular ejection, delaying pulmonic (P2) closure and thereby widening the physiologic splitting of S2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, augmenting venous return to the right heart. The larger right ventricular volume prolongs right ventricular ejection, delaying pulmonic (P2) closure and thereby widening the physiologic splitting of S2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitral closure contributes to S1, not S2, so its timing cannot change the A2-P2 interval.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inspiration slightly reduces left-sided return and only modestly shortens left ventricular ejection; the main driver of the wider split is delayed P2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inspiration increases, not reduces, right ventricular filling because negative intrathoracic pressure draws more venous blood into the right heart.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Systemic vascular resistance does not fall meaningfully with each breath; the respiratory change in splitting comes from right heart filling.
